hints: Notice that both salts first do the same simple acid-base reaction to make HX, so focus on what happens to that HX afterwards.

Look at the extra products with NaI: $\text{I}_2$ forms from $\text{I}^-$ while $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ form from concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, so one species is oxidised and the other is reduced.
Think about which halide ion loses electrons more easily to reduce sulfur from +6 to lower oxidation states, and why size down Group 17 matters.
walkthrough:
**Spot the common first step**

Both solids first act as bases toward concentrated sulfuric acid. This is a simple proton transfer to make the hydrogen halide.

$$\text{NaX} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HX}$$

**Compare what happens next**

With $\text{NaCl}$, the reaction stops at $\text{HCl}$. With $\text{NaI}$, the $\text{HI}$ first formed does not survive. It is oxidised to $\text{I}_2$ while the sulfur in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is reduced.

$$2\text{HI} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Link to reducing strength**

Reduction of S(+6) to $\text{SO}_2$ (+4), to $\text{S}$ (0) and even to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ (-2) needs a good electron donor. $\text{I}^-$ is larger than $\text{Cl}^-$ with its outer electron further from the nucleus and less tightly held, so it loses electrons much more easily.

In short, $\text{I}^-$ is a stronger reducing agent than $\text{Cl}^-$, so only $\text{HI}$ reduces the acid further.

options.A: Incorrect. Chlorine is more electronegative and a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, so $\text{Cl}_2$ displaces $\text{I}_2$, not the reverse. $\text{Cl}^-$ cannot oxidise $\text{I}^-$ or displace iodine, and this has nothing to do with the reduction of sulfuric acid.
options.B: Incorrect. Volatility is not the cause of the extra products. In fact $\text{HCl}$ (b.p. -85 C) is more volatile than $\text{HI}$ (b.p. -35 C), but both escape as gases. The key difference is redox chemistry, shown by $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, not boiling point.
options.C: Correct. $\text{I}^-$ is a better reducing agent than $\text{Cl}^-$ because the ion is larger and loses an electron more readily. It reduces S(VI) in concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ while itself being oxidised to $\text{I}_2$. $\text{Cl}^-$ is too weak a reducing agent to do this, so only $\text{HCl}$ forms.
options.D: Incorrect. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ can act as a dehydrating agent (removing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from carbohydrates or hydrated salts), but no dehydration is happening here. The formation of $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ shows reduction of sulfur, so the acid is acting as an oxidising agent, not a dehydrating agent.
